record.name: HBF: a read-oriented tier and its evidence boundary
record.shortName: HBF: a read-oriented tier and its evidence boundary
record.role: Distinguish an announced HBF interface/capacity specification from validated workload behavior.
record.description: High Bandwidth Flash proposes a NAND-based tier near the processor, alongside the existing memory hierarchy. SK hynix’s August 2026 announcement describes up to 512 GB and bandwidth grades of approximately 0.4–3.0 TB/s, with UCIe connectivity. These are reported specification boundaries, not proof of sustained throughput on a deployed inference system. A capacity and read-bandwidth headline leaves access latency, request granularity, concurrency, write service and host software to be examined. NAND-based capacity can be attractive for read-heavy state, but it does not acquire DRAM semantics merely by sharing a package or a fast link.
mechanism: Identify the source date and distinguish technical specification, sample, qualified component and shipping system.
Map the processor link, HBF controller and NAND array as separate interfaces; use the same transfer direction and byte convention.
Request latency, granularity, concurrency and read/write conditions before treating the headline rate as usable.
Keep mutable working state and recovery requirements in the placement contract rather than assuming every tensor can move to flash.
Measure application-level correctness, latency and energy on a named integration before claiming a deployment benefit.

science.title: Minimum bulk-read transfer time
science.explanation: Moving V payload bytes cannot take less than V/B at usable bandwidth B, even before initial access, scheduling or contention.
science.assumptions: Single direction with compatible decimal units; B is a sustained payload assumption, not automatically an advertised interface maximum.

record.tradeoff: More near-compute capacity may reduce remote movement, while page access, writes and integration requirements can move the performance bottleneck.
record.whyAI: Large read-mostly parameter pools are a possible use case; they require a software and system plan that accounts for access behavior.
record.misconception: An interface/specification announcement and a measured shipping-system result are different evidence states.

record.engineeringExample: Synthetic payload-only calculation: reading 100 GB at an assumed sustained 1 TB/s requires at least 0.1 s. No setup, concurrency loss or other work is included. The assumed usable rate is not a measured HBF benchmark.
record.evidenceNotes: SK hynix and Sandisk identify the August 2026 milestone as specification release. The atlas has not verified a volume-shipping deployment from these announcements. Missing access metrics remain unknown rather than receiving SSD or HBM defaults.
